messages.text: hey, can you explain Le Chatelier's principle in plain english? i keep mixing up which way the equilibrium shifts

Sure. Think of an equilibrium as a seesaw that wants to stay level. If you disturb it, the system shifts to partly undo what you did. Add more reactant and the position moves toward the products to use it up; remove a product and it moves right to make more. Raise the pressure and it favours the side with fewer gas molecules. Heating favours the endothermic direction.
ok so adding reactant = shift right, and removing product also = shift right?
Exactly, both push the equilibrium to the right. Adding product or removing reactant would push it left. A catalyst changes nothing about the position, it only gets you to equilibrium faster.

The tricky one is denn, which means roughly the same as weil but does not move the verb: "Ich bleibe zu Hause, denn ich bin müde." A quick test is to ask whether the clause could stand alone with the verb in second position; if yes, you probably need denn.

messages.text: hey quick postgres q. mujhe har merchant_id ki latest settlement row chahiye, abhi subquery with max(created_at) use kar raha hoon and its crawling on 40m rows

For 'latest row per group' Postgres has a neat tool: DISTINCT ON. Try SELECT DISTINCT ON (merchant_id) * FROM settlements ORDER BY merchant_id, created_at DESC; and back it with a composite index on (merchant_id, created_at DESC) so it can skip the sort. If you only need a few columns, select just those to keep it cheap.

Create the index with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_settlements_merchant_created ON settlements (merchant_id, created_at DESC); so you don't lock the table, then rerun EXPLAIN ANALYZE to confirm an index scan.

Use pg_isready in the healthcheck and add a start_period so early failures don't count. Something like interval 5s, timeout 3s, retries 10, start_period 30s usually settles it. Also make dependent services use condition: service_healthy.

messages.text: hey quick german grammar q. when do i use dem vs den? i always mix them up

Both depend on case and gender. "Dem" is the dative for masculine and neuter nouns (dem Koch, dem Kind), while "den" is the accusative for masculine nouns (den Koch) and also the dative plural (den Köchen, where the noun gets an extra -n). A quick test: ask "to whom?" for the dative and "whom or what?" for the accusative. In "Ich gebe dem Koch das Messer" the cook receives the knife, so it is dative.

Sure: 1) Ich zeige dem Gast die Speisekarte. 2) Die Köchin gibt den Kindern Suppe. 3) Er schneidet den Lauch. Translate them and tell me which one is dative singular, which is dative plural and which is accusative.
1 = i show the guest the menu (dative sing), 2 = the cook gives the kids soup (dative plural), 3 = he cuts the leek, accusative. right?
All three correct, well done. You even spotted the extra -n in "den Kindern". In sentence 3, "den Lauch" is accusative because the leek is the direct object of the cutting.

Multiply everything by 40/12, about 3.33: flour 2000 g, milk 1200 g, butter 300 g, salt 40 g, yeast about 67 g. Yeast scales a little less than linearly in big batches, so start with 55-60 g and adjust after a test bake. Also check that your mixer bowl can take roughly 3.6 kg of dough.
